candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control client-needs subcategory (10–16% of items); this item tests prevention of injury from invasive neurologic drainage equipment and recognition of unsafe device manipulation.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Prevention of overdrainage and neurologic harm during external lumbar CSF drainage
candidate.educational_objective: Maintain a gravity-dependent lumbar CSF drain at its prescribed level and avoid independent lowering of the system, because drain height influences the pressure gradient and excessive drainage can cause clinically important complications.

options.A: Maintain the drainage system at the prescribed level and recheck the setup after position changes rather than lowering it independently to increase drainage
options.B: Lower the drainage chamber whenever output decreases, regardless of the prescribed level or the client's neurologic status
options.C: Allow unrestricted drainage because drain height does not influence the pressure gradient or drainage volume
options.D: Remove the lumbar drain independently when the client reports a headache

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Contemporary lumbar-CSF-drain literature demonstrates that gravity-dependent drainage can be controlled by the vertical level of the drainage system and that excessive drainage can produce low-CSF-pressure symptoms and serious neurologic complications. Recent clinical protocols adjust drain height in response to pressure and drainage goals rather than treating the height as arbitrary. Therefore the nurse should preserve the prescribed level and reassess the setup after repositioning instead of independently lowering the system to accelerate drainage. B and C disregard the gravity/pressure relationship and can increase overdrainage risk. D exceeds nursing authority and bypasses evaluation of a potential complication. No universal centimeter setting is asserted because drainage targets and leveling protocols are condition- and institution-specific.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current peer-reviewed lumbar-drain literature directly supports that gravity-dependent drain height affects drainage/pressure gradient and that controlled leveling and close monitoring are used to reduce overdrainage risk.
candidate.source_document_title: The drainage volume control by elevation of drainage height versus head down tilt in supine position for management of cerebrospinal fluid leakage following lumbar posterior surgery; Impact of lumbar cerebrospinal fluid drainage to control intracranial hypertension in patients with severe traumatic brain injury
candidate.source_locator: 2024 CSF-leak study → Methods/Discussion: elevation of the drainage system was used to control drainage volume and maintain CSF pressure/volume; excessive or rapid CSF drainage can produce low-pressure symptoms. 2024 severe-TBI lumbar-drain cohort → nurse protocol: drain connected to a sterile collection bag with the pressure gradient set by system height; height was adjusted according to ICP and CSF drainage, with drainage stopped for concerning neurologic changes and close monitoring used to avoid overdrainage.
candidate.source_organization: Peer-reviewed neurosurgical literature indexed by the National Library of Medicine
candidate.source_version_date: Peer-reviewed studies published 2024; current literature checked 2026-08-18
candidate.stem: A client has a gravity-dependent lumbar cerebrospinal-fluid drain with a prescribed drainage level. Which nursing action is safest?
